blogs.title: When the Satirist Orders the Original: Transformative Use After a Self‑Generated Work
blogs.description: This post dissects the Second Circuit’s ruling that Jimmy Kimmel’s parody was “transformative” even though Kimmel himself requested and commissioned George Santos to produce the videos on Cameo. By focusing on the “reasonable observer” standard rather than subjective intent, the court affirmed that a work can still be highly transformative when used for commentary or criticism. The article will explore how this decision fits within recent fair‑use jurisprudence, offers guidance to creators who may be asked to generate content that later becomes fodder for parody, and warns about potential pitfalls when commissioning works intended for satirical reuse.

blogs.title: Good Faith Is No Longer a Shield: The Decline of Harper & Row’s ‘good‑faith’ Standard in Fair‑Use Analysis
blogs.description: Santos v. Kimmel revisits Harper & Row’s old dictum that “fair use presupposes good faith,” only to find it largely abandoned by contemporary courts. This blog examines how Judge Lohier’s opinion distances modern fair‑use theory from any substantive good‑faith requirement, aligning instead with recent decisions that treat bad‑faith behavior as immaterial when the four statutory factors favor fair use. It will trace the doctrinal shift from Harpers’ era through cases like Authors Guild v. Google and Andy Warhol Found., discussing what litigants can now expect when alleging bad‑faith conduct in copyright disputes.

blogs.title: Contract Claims vs. Copyright Preemption: Why Santos’s Breach‑of‑Contract Theory Was Doomed
blogs.description: The appellate court dismissed Santos’s breach‑of‑contract and implied‑contract claims on preemption grounds, reasoning that they were “qualitatively different” but still fell within the exclusive domain of the Copyright Act. This article unpacks the preemption analysis applied by the Second Circuit, contrasts it with prior rulings such as Melendez v. Sirius XM Radio, and evaluates how this approach limits plaintiffs’ ability to sidestep federal preemption via state‑law contract theories—particularly in disputes involving digital platforms and celebrity content.

blogs.title: Third‑Party Beneficiaries and Platform Terms of Service: Lessons From Santos’s Failed Claim Against Cameo’s Contract
blogs.description: Santos argued that Kimmel breached Cameo’s Terms of Service, seeking to enforce those provisions as a non‑signatory third party. The court rejected this claim, emphasizing Illinois’ strong presumption against imposing contractual benefits on outsiders unless expressly declared. This blog will examine the legal standards governing third‑party beneficiary status under both Illinois and New York law, assess how platforms can structure their TOS to avoid unintended liability, and explore broader implications for celebrities who attempt to enforce platform agreements against individuals who never agreed to them.
